definition: A single instruction the program carries out, ending in a semicolon. Declaring a variable, calling a method and assigning a value are all statements.
Zero or more statements wrapped in `{ }` braces. Blocks are the bodies of methods, loops and if statements, and each one is a scope for the variables declared inside it.
The method the runtime calls to start the program. With top-level statements the compiler writes `Main` for you, but it still exists.
A modern C# feature that lets a file contain statements with no class or `Main` method around them - the compiler generates the `Main` method behind the scenes.
A named container that groups related types and keeps their names from clashing. `using System;` brings the `System` namespace into scope so you can write `Console` instead of `System.Console`.
A line at the top of a file that imports a namespace so its types can be used by their short names. Not to be confused with a `using` statement, which disposes a resource.
The tool that checks the whole program for mistakes and translates it into runnable code before anything executes. Because C# is compiled, many errors are found before the program ever runs.
Every variable has a fixed type known at compile time, and the compiler refuses to mix them up. You cannot store text in an `int`.
A named slot that stores a value of one particular type. Declared with a type and a name, and given a value with `=`.
What kind of value a variable holds and what you can do with it: `int` for whole numbers, `double` for decimals, `bool` for true/false, `char` for a single character, `string` for text.
A named value fixed at compile time that can never change, declared with `const`. Use one instead of a magic number so the meaning is clear.
Lets the compiler work out a local variable's type from the value you assign. The type is still fixed - `var` is not 'any type', it is 'you can see the type from the right-hand side'.
Building a string by putting expressions inside braces in a string prefixed with `$`. Cleaner than joining pieces with `+`.
A code after a colon inside an interpolated string that controls how a value is printed - `:N2` for two decimal places with thousands separators, `:C` for currency, `:P` for a percentage.
The class for text input and output in a terminal program. `WriteLine` prints a line, `Write` prints without a newline, `ReadLine` reads a line the user types (always as a `string`).
Turning text into a value of another type. `int.Parse` throws if the text is not a number; `int.TryParse` returns `false` instead, which is what you want for user input.
A symbol that combines values into a new one: arithmetic (`+ - * / %`), comparison (`== != < >`), logical (`&& || !`) and assignment (`= += -=`).
Anything that produces a value: a literal, a variable, a method call, or operators combined. `age >= 18` is an expression whose value is a `bool`.
Dividing one `int` by another throws away the remainder: `7 / 2` is `3`, not `3.5`. Make one side a `double` if you want the decimal answer.
The `%` operator gives the remainder after integer division. GCSE pseudocode calls it `MOD`. Handy for 'is it even?' (`n % 2 == 0`) and wrapping around.
With `&&` and `||`, the right-hand side is only evaluated if it can still change the answer. So `list != null && list.Count > 0` is safe - the `Count` is never read on a `null` list.
A compact if/else that produces a value: `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`.
Choosing which code runs based on a condition - `if`, `else if`, `else` and `switch`. One of the three building blocks of every program alongside sequence and iteration.
Selection with many branches on one value. The `switch` statement uses `case` labels; the newer switch expression returns a value directly and works well with pattern matching.
Testing a value against a shape - a type, a range, a property value or a tuple - and pulling pieces out at the same time. Used with `is` and `switch`.
Repeating a block of code. C# has `for` (count-controlled), `while` and `do-while` (condition-controlled) and `foreach` (over every item in a collection).
A loop that visits every element of a collection in turn without you managing an index. Works with anything that is `IEnumerable`.
`break` leaves the innermost loop (or `switch`) immediately; `continue` skips the rest of this pass and goes straight to the next iteration.
A fixed-size, zero-indexed sequence of values all of the same type. `Length` never changes once created; use `List<T>` when you need to grow.
The position of an element, counted from 0. The last valid index is `Length - 1`; going past it throws `IndexOutOfRangeException` - the classic off-by-one bug.
A bug where a loop runs one time too many or too few, usually from mixing up `<` and `<=` or forgetting arrays start at 0.
A grid with a fixed number of rows and columns, declared with a comma: `int[,]`. Every row is the same length.
An array whose elements are themselves arrays, so each row can be a different length: `int[][]`.
A sequence of characters. Strings are immutable - methods like `ToUpper` or `Replace` return a new string rather than changing the original.
A single character in single quotes, such as `'a'` or `'7'`. A string is made of chars, and you can index into it: `name[0]`.
A mutable buffer for building up a large string piece by piece. Much faster than repeated `+` in a loop, because it does not create a new string each time.
A named block of code you can call. Takes parameters, may return a value, and lets you name and reuse a piece of logic. GCSE pseudocode calls them subroutines, functions or procedures.
example: static int Square(int n) => n * n;

definition: A variable listed in a method's declaration that receives a value when the method is called. The value passed in is the argument.
The result a method hands back to its caller with the `return` keyword. A method declared `void` returns nothing.
A method's name plus the number, types and order of its parameters. Two methods in the same class may share a name only if their signatures differ.
Defining several methods with the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler picks the one that matches the arguments.
example: void Print(int n) {} void Print(string s) {}

definition: A parameter with a default value that the caller may leave out. Named arguments (`Greet(name: "Ada")`) let you pass them in any order.
example: void Greet(string name, bool shout = false)

definition: Modifiers that make a parameter refer to the caller's variable rather than a copy. `out` means the method must assign it - the way `TryParse` gives you the number back.
Changing a value from one type to another. Widening (`int` to `double`) is implicit and safe; narrowing (`double` to `int`) needs an explicit cast and can lose data.
A helper with methods like `Convert.ToInt32` and `Convert.ToDouble` that convert between types, including from strings, with rounding rather than truncation.
A `static` class of maths helpers: `Math.Sqrt`, `Math.Pow`, `Math.Round`, `Math.Abs`, `Math.Max` and `Math.Min`. Note `Math.Round` uses banker's rounding by default.
The class for pseudo-random numbers. `Random.Shared.Next(1, 7)` gives 1 to 6 - the upper bound is exclusive. Seed one for repeatable results in tests.
An object that describes something going wrong at run time - a missing file, a bad cast, division by zero. Thrown with `throw` and caught with `try`/`catch`; unhandled, it crashes the program.
example: throw new ArgumentException("Age cannot be negative");

definition: The structure for handling exceptions: code that might fail goes in `try`, recovery in `catch` (most specific type first), and `finally` always runs for clean-up.
The list of method calls that were active when an exception was thrown, printed newest first. Read it top-down to find the line that failed.
Finding and fixing bugs. A debugger lets you pause on a breakpoint, inspect variables and step through one line at a time - faster than sprinkling `Console.WriteLine` everywhere.

A mistake the compiler catches before the program runs, such as a missing semicolon or assigning a `string` to an `int`. Contrast with a runtime error (an exception) or a logic error (wrong answer, no crash).
The program runs without crashing but gives the wrong answer - the hardest kind of bug, found with tests and careful reading, not the compiler.
Organising a program around objects that bundle data (fields) with the behaviour that works on it (methods). Built on four ideas: abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
A blueprint that describes what a kind of object stores and can do. Defines fields, properties, constructors and methods; objects are made from it with `new`.
example: class Student { public string Name { get; set; } }

definition: One concrete thing made from a class with `new` - an instance. Each object has its own copy of the instance fields.
A special method with the class's name that runs when an object is created, usually to set the initial values of its fields. A class can have several (overloaded) constructors.
A variable declared inside a class that belongs to each object. Usually kept `private` and exposed through a property.

A member that looks like a field from outside but runs code (`get` / `set`) when read or written, so a class can validate or compute values. `{ get; set; }` is an auto-property; `init` lets it be set only during construction.
example: public int Age { get; private set; }

definition: A keyword referring to the current object - the instance the method was called on. Used to tell a field from a parameter of the same name, or to pass the object elsewhere.
Showing what something does while hiding how. You call `list.Sort()` without knowing the algorithm. Interfaces and abstract classes are how C# expresses it.
Keeping an object's data private and controlling all access through methods and properties, so the object can guarantee its own rules (a balance can never go negative).
A keyword that says who can see a member: `public` (anyone), `private` (this class only), `protected` (this class and subclasses), `internal` (this project). Default for members is `private`.
Making a new class from an existing one so it gets all the base class's members and can add or change behaviour. Written `class Dog : Animal`. Every class ultimately inherits from `object`.
Refers to the parent class: `base(...)` in a constructor calls the parent's constructor, `base.Method()` calls the parent's version of an overridden method.
'Many forms': calling the same method on different objects and getting behaviour appropriate to each. A `List<Shape>` can hold circles and squares, and `shape.Area()` runs the right code for each.
Marks a method in a base class that subclasses are allowed to replace with `override`. Without `virtual`, a subclass method of the same name just hides the parent's.
Providing a subclass's own version of a `virtual` or `abstract` method from its parent, using the `override` keyword. Different from overloading, which is same name with different parameters.
example: public override double Area() => Math.PI * r * r;

definition: A class that cannot be instantiated and exists to be inherited from. May contain `abstract` methods - declared with no body - that every concrete subclass must `override`.
example: abstract class Shape { public abstract double Area(); }

definition: Stops a class being inherited from, or an `override` being overridden further. Records and most well-designed classes are `sealed` unless inheritance is intended.
A contract listing members a type promises to provide, with no implementation of its own. A class can implement many interfaces; names start with `I` by convention (`IComparable`, `IEnumerable`).
A type whose variable holds the value itself - `int`, `double`, `bool`, `char`, structs and enums. Copying a value type copies the data; two copies are independent.
A type whose variable holds a reference (an address) to an object on the heap - classes, strings, arrays, delegates. Copying the variable copies the reference, so both point at the same object.
A lightweight value type you define yourself, good for small immutable data like a point or a colour. Copied on assignment; cannot inherit from another struct or class.
example: struct Point { public int X; public int Y; }

definition: A type with a fixed set of named values, backed by an integer. Use one instead of magic numbers or strings for things like days or states.
example: enum Suit { Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs, Spades }

definition: A type designed for holding data: it gets value-based equality, a readable `ToString` and a `with` expression for making changed copies for free. Positional records declare properties in the header.
An object whose state cannot change after it is created. Safer to share and reason about; you make changed copies instead of mutating. Strings, records and `readonly` fields are all immutable.
A field modifier meaning it can only be assigned in the declaration or a constructor. Unlike `const`, the value can be computed at run time.

Reference equality asks 'same object?'; value equality asks 'same contents?'. Classes get reference equality by default; override `Equals` and `GetHashCode` together (or use a `record`) to get value equality.
The method every object has for describing itself as text. Override it so `Console.WriteLine(myObject)` prints something useful instead of the type name.
Defining what `+`, `==`, `<` and so on mean for your own type, with a `static operator` method. Sensible for maths-like types (Money, Vector), confusing for anything else.
example: public static Money operator +(Money a, Money b)

definition: A member that belongs to the class rather than to any object - one copy shared by all. Called on the type name, like `Math.Sqrt`. A `static` class can only contain `static` members.
Building a class out of other objects it holds as fields ('has-a') rather than inheriting from them ('is-a'). Usually more flexible - prefer it unless the is-a relationship is genuine.
A weaker has-a relationship where the parts can exist independently of the whole - a Team has Players, but the Players survive if the Team is deleted. Drawn with a hollow diamond in UML.
Unified Modelling Language - a standard way to draw the classes in a design, their members and how they relate (inheritance arrows, association lines, multiplicity).
How much one class depends on the details of another. Low (loose) coupling is the goal: change one class and the others do not break. Interfaces and dependency injection reduce it.
How focused a class is on one job. High cohesion is good: everything in the class belongs together. A 'Utils' class that does everything has low cohesion.
Five design principles: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion. Together they push towards small, focused, loosely coupled classes.

A named, reusable solution to a common design problem - Strategy (swap an algorithm via an interface), Observer (events), Factory (a method that decides which class to create), Repository (hide the data store).
A pattern that guarantees exactly one instance of a class exists and gives global access to it. Easy to overuse - it is a global variable in disguise, which makes testing harder.
A resizable array. `Add`, `Remove`, `Insert`, `Contains`, `IndexOf` and an indexer, plus `Sort` and everything LINQ offers. The default collection to reach for.
Any object that holds a group of items - arrays, `List<T>`, `Dictionary`, `HashSet`, `Stack`, `Queue`. Most live in `System.Collections.Generic` and all can be iterated with `foreach`.
A collection of key/value pairs with near-instant lookup by key. Keys must be unique. Use `TryGetValue` to look up safely without an exception.
example: var ages = new Dictionary<string, int>(); ages["Ada"] = 36;

definition: A collection of unique items with fast `Contains`, `Add` and `Remove`, and set operations like `UnionWith` and `IntersectWith`. Order is not guaranteed.
A last-in, first-out collection: `Push` adds to the top, `Pop` removes from the top, `Peek` looks without removing. Used for undo, bracket matching and the call stack itself.
A first-in, first-out collection: `Enqueue` joins the back, `Dequeue` leaves the front. Used for print queues, breadth-first search and anything processed in arrival order.
A sequence of nodes where each node holds a value and a reference to the next (and, if doubly linked, the previous). Cheap to insert or remove in the middle; slow to reach the nth item.
One element in a linked structure - a linked list, tree or graph - holding a value plus references to its neighbours.
Writing a class or method once with a placeholder type `T` that is filled in when it is used. `List<T>` works for any `T`. Constraints like `where T : IComparable<T>` say what `T` must support.
example: T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>

definition: The interface for 'a sequence you can loop over'. Anything `foreach` accepts is `IEnumerable`, and every LINQ method works on it. It promises only forward, one-at-a-time access.
Turns a method into an iterator: each `yield return` hands out one item and pauses until the caller asks for the next. Lets you produce sequences lazily, even infinite ones.
example: IEnumerable<int> Evens() { for (int i = 0; ; i += 2) yield return i; }

definition: A LINQ query or iterator does no work when you write it - only when something enumerates it. Call `ToList()` to run it once and keep the results.
A set of methods for querying any sequence in a declarative style: `Where` filters, `Select` projects (transforms), `OrderBy` sorts, and many more chain together.
Transforming each item of a sequence into something else with `Select` - names into lengths, orders into totals, objects into anonymous types.
A throwaway class the compiler creates from `new { Name = ..., Age = ... }`, handy for shaping LINQ results without declaring a class. Only usable inside the method that makes it.
Collapsing a sequence to a single value: `Count`, `Sum`, `Average`, `Min`, `Max`, or the general `Aggregate` for anything else.
Splits a sequence into groups sharing a key - students by class, orders by month - each group being a key plus its items. `Join` matches items from two sequences on a key.

A type that holds a reference to a method, so methods can be stored in variables and passed as arguments. `Func<T, TResult>` returns a value, `Action<T>` returns `void`, `Predicate<T>` returns `bool`.
example: Func<int, int> square = n => n * n;

definition: A method you hand to some other code so it can call you back later - when a button is clicked, when a download finishes, for each item it processes. Delegates and lambdas are how C# passes them.
An inline, unnamed method written as `parameters => body`. Used everywhere in LINQ and event handling.
A lambda that uses a variable from the surrounding method 'captures' it and keeps it alive - the lambda can read and change it even after the method has returned.
A one-line method or property written with `=>` instead of a block: `int Double(int n) => n * 2;`. Same meaning, less ceremony.
A method that takes another method as a parameter or returns one - `Where`, `Select` and `Sort(comparison)` all are. Composing small pure functions is the heart of functional style.
A member a class raises to announce something happened, which any number of listeners can subscribe to with `+=`. Built on delegates; the publisher does not know who is listening.
A `static` method that can be called as if it were an instance method on another type, thanks to `this` on its first parameter. It is how LINQ adds `Where` and `Select` to every `IEnumerable`.
example: static bool IsEven(this int n) => n % 2 == 0;

definition: The value meaning 'no object here'. Using a member on a `null` reference throws `NullReferenceException` - historically the most common bug in C#.
A compiler feature where a reference type is non-null unless you write `?` after it (`string?`). The compiler then warns wherever a possibly-null value is used without a check.
A value type that can also be `null`, written `int?`. Check `HasValue` or compare to `null` before reading `.Value`.
`?.` calls a member only if the object is not `null`, otherwise the whole expression is `null`. Saves a nest of `if` checks.
`??` gives a fallback when the left side is `null`: `name ?? "Unknown"`. `??=` assigns the fallback only if the variable is currently `null`.
A lightweight bundle of several values with optional names, without declaring a type. Handy for returning two things from a method.
Unpacking a tuple or record into separate variables in one line: `var (x, y) = point;`. Any type can support it by providing a `Deconstruct` method.
Your own exception class, inheriting from `Exception`, so callers can catch a specific failure by type. Name it with the `Exception` suffix and give it a useful message.
`catch (X e) when (condition)` catches only when the condition holds. To rethrow and keep the stack trace, use bare `throw;`, not `throw e;`.
The interface for objects holding something that must be released promptly - a file handle, a network connection. Its one method, `Dispose`, does the clean-up; a `using` statement calls it for you.
Guarantees `Dispose` is called on an `IDisposable` when the block ends, even if an exception is thrown. `using var file = File.OpenRead(path);` disposes at the end of the enclosing scope.
The part of the .NET runtime that automatically frees memory for objects nothing references any more. You never delete objects by hand - but you do still `Dispose` unmanaged resources.
The two regions of memory a program uses. The stack holds local variables and method calls, freed automatically as methods return; the heap holds objects, freed by the garbage collector.
Reading and writing files. `File.ReadAllText` / `WriteAllLines` for small files, `StreamReader` / `StreamWriter` for line by line, `Path.Combine` to build paths safely, `Directory` to list folders.
JavaScript Object Notation - a text format for structured data. `JsonSerializer.Serialize` turns an object into JSON; `Deserialize<T>` turns it back.
Turning an object into a form that can be saved or sent - JSON, XML, bytes - and back again (deserialization). Watch out for cycles, private fields and versioning.
Starting slow work (a download, a file read) without blocking the thread while it completes. Mark the method `async`, and `await` the `Task` - the method pauses without freezing the program.
An object representing work that will finish in the future, possibly with a result (`Task<T>`). `await` it to get the result; `Task.WhenAll` waits for several at once.
Metadata attached to code in square brackets - `[Obsolete]`, `[JsonIgnore]`, `[Fact]` - that tools and libraries read at run time via reflection.
Code that inspects types at run time - listing a class's properties, reading attributes, creating objects by name. Powerful and slow; it is how serializers and test frameworks work.

Describes how an algorithm's running time or memory grows with input size `n`, ignoring constants. `O(1)` constant, `O(log n)` logarithmic, `O(n)` linear, `O(n log n)`, `O(n²)` quadratic, `O(2ⁿ)` exponential.
A precise, finite sequence of steps that solves a problem. Judged on correctness first, then time and space complexity.
A way of organising data so particular operations are fast - arrays for indexing, hash tables for lookup, trees for ordered data, graphs for networks.
Checking each item in turn until you find the target. Works on unsorted data; `O(n)` time.
Searching sorted data by repeatedly halving the range: look at the middle, discard the half that cannot contain the target. `O(log n)` - a million items in about 20 steps.
Putting items in order. Bubble, insertion and selection sort are simple and `O(n²)`; merge sort and quicksort are `O(n log n)` and what real libraries use.
A divide-and-conquer sort: split the list in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves. Always `O(n log n)` and stable, at the cost of extra memory.
A divide-and-conquer sort: pick a pivot, partition items into less-than and greater-than, then sort each side recursively. `O(n log n)` on average, in place, but `O(n²)` with a bad pivot.
A method that calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. Every recursive method needs a base case that stops, or it recurses until the stack overflows.
example: int Fact(int n) => n <= 1 ? 1 : n * Fact(n - 1);

definition: The runtime's record of which methods are currently running, each with its local variables. A call pushes a frame; a return pops it. Deep recursion grows it fast.
The crash when the call stack runs out of room - almost always recursion with a missing or unreachable base case.
A tree where each node has at most two children, everything in the left subtree is smaller and everything in the right is larger. Search, insert and delete are `O(log n)` when balanced.

Visiting every node of a tree in a defined order. In-order (left, node, right) gives a BST's items sorted; pre-order (node, left, right) copies the structure; post-order (left, right, node) deletes safely.
A set of vertices (nodes) joined by edges. Edges may be directed or undirected, weighted or not. Stored as an adjacency list (each node's neighbours) or adjacency matrix (a grid).
Exploring a graph level by level from a start node using a queue. Finds the shortest path in number of edges on an unweighted graph.
Exploring a graph by following one path as far as it goes before backtracking, using recursion or an explicit stack. Good for detecting cycles and exploring mazes.
Finds the cheapest path from one node to all others in a weighted graph with no negative edges, always expanding the closest unvisited node next (a priority queue makes that fast).
A queue where `Dequeue` always returns the item with the lowest priority value rather than the oldest. .NET's `PriorityQueue` is a binary heap; Dijkstra's algorithm depends on one.

A structure that turns a key into an array index with a hash function, giving `O(1)` average lookup. Two keys landing in the same bucket is a collision, handled by chaining or probing. `Dictionary` and `HashSet` are hash tables.
A function that maps data of any size to a fixed-size number. Hash tables use a fast one (`GetHashCode`); security uses a cryptographic one (`SHA-256`) that is practically impossible to reverse.
An independent path of execution inside a program. Several threads can run at once on different cores. Sharing data between them safely is the hard part.
Doing more than one thing at a time - or appearing to. Parallelism uses several cores at once for CPU work; asynchrony frees a thread while waiting for I/O.
A bug where the result depends on the exact timing of threads - two threads incrementing the same counter can lose updates. Fixed by locking or by not sharing mutable state.

A statement that lets only one thread at a time run a block of code, protecting shared data. `Interlocked` offers cheaper atomic operations for simple counters. Two threads each waiting for the other's lock is a deadlock.
Measuring how long code really takes rather than guessing. `Stopwatch` for quick checks, `BenchmarkDotNet` for serious numbers. Measure before you optimise.
A view over a slice of memory - part of an array or string - with no copying and no heap allocation. Used in performance-sensitive code to avoid creating garbage.
Boxing wraps a value type in an object on the heap (`int` stored as `object`); unboxing takes it out again. Both cost time and memory - generics exist largely to avoid it.
Never store passwords - store a slow, salted hash of them (PBKDF2, bcrypt, Argon2) and compare hashes at login. A salt is random data added so identical passwords hash differently.
Scrambling data so only someone with the key can read it. Symmetric (AES) uses one shared key; asymmetric (RSA) uses a public/private pair. Unlike hashing, encryption is reversible.
Never trusting data from outside the program. Check length, range and format; use parameterised queries so user text can never be run as SQL (injection).
Giving a class the things it depends on (through its constructor) instead of letting it create them. Depend on interfaces, and you can swap a real database for a fake one in tests.
A small automated test that checks one piece of code gives the expected result. Frameworks like `xUnit` run them all on every build, so a change that breaks something is caught immediately.
Splitting a program into layers - user interface, business logic, data access - each depending only on the layer beneath. Keeps concerns separate so each part can change or be tested alone.
The region of code where a variable can be seen - from its declaration to the end of the enclosing block. A local declared inside a loop does not exist outside it.
